Hi Evelyne,
 Can you try to update GenomicRanges and methylKit and see if the error persists?. I guess you are subsetting methylRaw objects before tileMethylCounts otherwise it shouldn't contain levels that are not present in the GRanges conversion.

Best,
Altuna

On Thu, Nov 28, 2013 at 10:58 AM, <evelyne.c...@gmail.com> wrote:

> Hi Altuna,
>
> I am a colleague of Cindy and investigated her issue more in depth.
> I found that because we are working with rather short scaffolds, our g.meth object within regionalize.R (tileMethylCounts) contains more seqname levels than there actually are. This will then cause regionCounts to be executed on chromosomes which do not exist, resulting in empty data.frames and thus NA errors.
>
> The quickfix for our error is to replace line 336 in regionalize.R:
>
> chrs   =IRanges::levels(seqnames(g.meth))
>  by
>
> chrs   =unique(seqnames(g.meth))
>
> I am no expert in the GenomicRanges package, but maybe there is also a function to drop the empty seqnames from the levels?

messages.subject: Re: meaning of "total otherC considered"?
messages.subject_clean: meaning of "total otherC considered"?
messages.body_plain:
OtherC refers to the non-CpG Cs. Converstion rate is calculated as number of Ts(non-methylated Cytosines) divided by coverage for each non-CpG cytosine. And the average conversion rate is the average of those values. For a cytosine to be included in this calculation it has to have at least 10X  coverage and the bases generating that coverage should have at least 20 phred score (if you haven't changed the default arguments).  If you believe non-CG methylation is prevalent in your organism and/or tissue you need to do spike-in controls to reliably measure the conversion rate.

Best,
Altuna

you can keep bases that are below 10X coverage in methylKit, then you can tile 50 bp windows. I don't think you can use eDMR because it is designed for clustering of DMCs based on distribution of distances between nearest CpGs and may be optimized for that assumption not for tiling windows (Sheng Li may comment on this)

you can do what you suggested in general, loosen the coverage threshold and tile windows over the genome, and as you say people do it. I don't know if the methylation estimates would be reliable with 3-4X coverage. To test that, you can take a high coverage whole-genome BS or RRBS data set, down-sample the coverage (aligned reads) to  3-4X and tile 50 bp windows, also tile 50 bp windows from the original set and check the correlation/scatter plot between these two sets. If they are very different, you need to get more coverage.

Best,
Altuna

Hi Altuna,
In the previous versions, I used the 'ID column' as a nifty index for all kinds of parsing outside of R. The format was ChrN.start.stop.BedNameField. I could do this because I always fed features in a bed file format with a name field.

I followed your suggestion and obtained the original "BedNameField" via the following steps:
# query is diff object, subject is feature object
test_findOverlaps<-as.matrix(findOverlaps(as(new_prom.refseq.diff,"GRanges"),new_prom.refseq.obj@listData$new_prom.refseq,type="equal",select="all"))
# get subject ID matching the query
new_prom.refseq.obj@listData$new_prom.refseq@elementMetadata@listData$name[test_findOverlaps[,2]]
# get subject ID matching the query and return data frame
new_prom.refseq.diff.id <http://new_prom.refseq.diff.id><-data.frame(new_prom.refseq.obj@listData$new_prom.refseq@elementMetadata@listData$name[test_findOverlaps[,2]],check.names=FALSE,stringsAsFactors=FALSE)
# change column name prior to write out
colnames(new_prom.refseq.diff.id <http://new_prom.refseq.diff.id>)<-c("new_prom.refseq.diff.id <http://new_prom.refseq.diff.id>")

Working this out led me to discover something about the new unite function. If a feature object has more than one entry sharing identical chromosome, start, stop, coordinates , unite behaves unexpectedly at region level.
for instance, I discovered my mouse promoter file contained three entries with identical chrom,start,stop (I had taken previous steps to remove such redundancies) :
chr3 104666423  104668423 NM_001253702 229681 +
chr3 104666423  104668423 NM_009797 12340 -
chr3 104666423  104668423 NM_153091 229681 +
Notice two are on the positive strand, one is on the negative strand. In a promoter region comparison of two pooled biological replicates per condition [methylBase obtained by pool(unite()) ], methylKit produced 81 separate entries total for the (+) coordinates [n = 54] and (-) coordinates [n = 27] in the methylBase and methylDiff objects. Only two entries are produced after I removed one of the (+) strand promoters and added 1 bp to the (-) strand promoter coordinates.

Regards,
Ben

Hi Ben,
Thanks for pointing this out. I would expect this from the new unite function, since it only merges on chr,start,end and strand. If there are duplicate coordinates, depending on the number of samples you will end up with more duplicates as you have observed.

It was nifty for me as well to add the name column to the id and do a merge based on that, but id column really inflates the memory footprint of the object and makes things harder when you have a lot of samples to deal with.

My advice would be that the users should check if their annotations/regions of interest have duplicated coordinates, and remove the ones that are duplicated. This is easy to do in GenomicRanges. Assume "gr" contains the regions of interest/annotations. The following removes the duplicated coordinates.

gr=gr[!duplicated(gr),]

Best,
Altuna
